title: The Team Respects What You Inspect
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay contends that when a leader personally measures something outside the usual dashboard of KPIs and OKRs, the act itself signals to the team what truly matters. Because most metrics are automated and impersonal, a leader who takes the initiative to inspect a new angle — say, onboarding effectiveness at the two-year mark, or participation rates in a new program — draws outsized attention and sparks conversation. The piece frames these ad hoc measurements as temporary, one-time snapshots rather than permanent KPIs, useful precisely because they redirect focus rather than replace the existing measurement system. It closes by encouraging leaders to invent a novel measure periodically to keep the team's attention on emerging priorities.
points: Automated metrics rarely carry the same weight as something a leader personally chooses to measure.
Whatever a leader closely observes or inspects becomes what the team treats as important.
One-off measurements — like output at the two-year mark or new-idea counts — can spotlight issues without becoming permanent KPIs.
These improvised metrics work because they are novel and prompt fresh conversation, not because they are statistically rigorous.
Leaders who stick only to established metrics lose a tool for signaling priorities to their teams.
quotes: But what impact does a leader have when they find a new way of looking at the team’s progress and gauge it themselves?
In most organizations, metrics are automated or computed by a support team and then made available to leaders on a periodic basis as they assess the health of the team.
Team members don’t hold in high regard any matter that doesn’t draw the attention and focus of their leader.
Just taking the time to closely observe any issue, process, or project will spotlight what the leader believes to be important.
Consider trying a novel measurement to start a brand-new conversation within your team.
